title: The Crow and the Swan
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Crow was filled with envy on seeing the beautiful white plumage of a Swan, and thought it was due to the water in which the Swan constantly bathed and swam. So he left the neighbourhood of the altars, where he got his living by picking up bits of the meat offered in sacrifice, and went and lived among the pools and streams. But though he bathed and washed his feathers many times a day, he didn't make them any whiter, and at last died of hunger into the bargain.
You may change your habits, but not your nature.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Crow envy about the Swan?
options: Her graceful way of swimming
Her loud, clear call
Her beautiful white plumage
Her large size compared to other birds

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Crow think causes the Swan's white feathers?
options: The water in which the Swan constantly bathed and swam
A special diet of certain plants
The Swan's habit of resting in the sun
A gift given to the Swan by the gods

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Crow used to get his living?
options: By stealing eggs from other birds' nests
By following farmers as they plowed their fields
By fishing for small creatures in shallow water
By picking up bits of meat offered in sacrifice near the altars

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Crow go to live instead?
options: Deep within a quiet forest
Among the pools and streams
Near a busy marketplace
Along a rocky mountainside

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Crow do many times a day in his new home?
options: Searches for meat near the altars
Calls out to other crows nearby
Bathes and washes his feathers
Watches the Swan swim in the distance

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Crow in the end?
options: He dies of hunger, and his feathers never turn white
He becomes just as white as the Swan
He returns to the altars and lives happily
He befriends the Swan and learns to swim well

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what mistake does the Crow make about the source of the Swan's whiteness?
options: He assumes the Swan bathes far more often than she actually does
He assumes the water near the altars was too dirty for white feathers
He assumes the Swan was born gray and slowly became white
He assumes a surface habit, like bathing, could change something that is actually part of the Swan's nature

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Crow end up dying of hunger?
options: He is too weak from constant bathing to search for food
He gives up his reliable source of food near the altars for a place that could not feed him
He is chased away from the pools by the Swan
He refuses to eat anything but meat from sacrifices

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "plumage" mean in "the beautiful white plumage of a Swan"?
options: A bird's call or song
A bird's nest
A bird's feathers
A bird's wingspan

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Changing your surface habits cannot change what you fundamentally are
Swans are naturally more graceful than crows in every way
Living near water always improves an animal's appearance
Envy is a harmless emotion as long as it inspires change

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what feeling does the Crow experience upon seeing the Swan?
options: Fear
Curiosity
Admiration without envy
Envy

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Crow leave behind when he moved to the pools and streams?
options: A nest he had built for years
The neighbourhood of the altars
A group of other crows
A steady supply of clean water

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how often does the Crow bathe in his new home?
options: Once a week
Only at night
Many times a day
Only during the summer

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the phrase "into the bargain" suggest about the Crow's death by hunger?
options: It was an additional loss on top of never achieving the white feathers he wanted
It was the only outcome the Crow had hoped for
It happened before he even reached the pools and streams
It was caused directly by the Swan's actions

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Crow's failure suggest about trying to imitate another creature's traits?
options: Any animal can achieve any appearance with enough effort
Water is the only requirement for white feathers
Imitating another creature always leads to social rejection
Copying surface behavior cannot grant qualities that come from a different underlying nature

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "neighbourhood" mean in "the neighbourhood of the altars"?
options: A group of people living together
The surrounding area near a place
A formal religious ceremony
A type of stone building

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Crow successfully becomes as white as a Swan after much bathing
A Swan teaches a Crow how to find food near the altars
A Crow abandons his reliable food source trying to turn white like a Swan, and starves without ever changing color
A Crow and a Swan become companions by the pools and streams
